coachMessages.text: It's your very first move of the game. Seven columns to choose from — but they are not all equal. Which one gives you the most ways to connect four later?

slides.infoProse: Every four-in-a-row runs through some set of columns and rows. A disc in the middle column sits inside far more possible horizontal, vertical, and diagonal lines than a disc on the edge — so it keeps the most winning paths alive. That is why the centre column is the strongest opening square: it is the only first move that lets Green force a win with perfect play. The four columns further from the centre are markedly weaker.

coachMessages.text: Here both players raced up the centre column, then Gray opened the next column over and Green answered on top. This is the '5-4' central-column opening — a known Green win.

slides.infoProse: This is the headline result of opening theory: central-column play wins, edge play doesn't. After both sides build up the centre column, Green is the only one who can threaten a horizontal connection on the third row nearby, while Gray's best threats sit on the diagonals through the centre. (Why the third row favours Green is exactly what the Odd Rows lesson explains later.) Green used that edge to shift into the neighbouring column and is already winning here — the position is fully resolved in Green's favour.

coachMessages.text: Green and Gray built three columns in parallel, each answering directly on top of the last disc. Simple moves, strong position.

slides.infoProse: Notice the shape: three columns, each filled by simply answering above the opponent's last disc. This is Allen's 'I play where you play' idea — when nothing sharper is available, playing directly on top of your opponent is often good enough, and it keeps the game easy to navigate. It is a shortcut, not a rule; you still have to check it against real threats as the game develops.

coachMessages.text: Why is the centre worth so much? Count the lines. The next cell up the centre column sits on 13 different four-in-a-row lines — a corner cell sits on just 3.

legendItems.label: Compare these two cells — count the lines through each

slides.infoProse: Here is the arithmetic behind the whole lesson. The board has 69 possible four-in-a-row windows — horizontal, vertical, and diagonal. The two middle cells of the centre column each lie on 13 of those windows, the most of any cell on the board, and even the centre column's bottom cell lies on 7. A corner cell lies on just 3. Every disc placed in the centre keeps far more winning lines alive than the same disc on the edge — that count is the reason the centre column is the strongest territory on the board.

socratic.goalPrompt: You move first — where is the strongest opening move?
socratic._boardInstructions: Empty board, Green (first player) to move. No overlays: nothing should hint at the answer before the student attempts it. Correct answer is the centre column (0-indexed col 3).

ask.text: You move first — where is the strongest opening move?
ask.text_es: Movés primero — ¿dónde está la jugada de apertura más fuerte?

wrong1.text: Not quite — look for the right square. Try again.
wrong1.text_es: No exactamente — buscá la casilla correcta. Intentalo de nuevo.

correct.text: Exactly — the centre column. It keeps the most winning paths alive.
correct.text_es: Exacto — la columna central. Mantiene vivas la mayor cantidad de caminos ganadores.

hint.text: Which column sits on the most possible four-in-a-row lines?
hint.text_es: ¿Qué columna se encuentra en la mayor cantidad de posibles líneas de cuatro en línea?
